bank: Banco de España and Global Finance & Technology Network
title: Spain and GFTN set out what a Europe–Latin America payments partnership would have to deliver
summary: Banco de España and the Global Finance & Technology Network have signed an agreement to develop a Madrid summit on financial cooperation between Europe and Latin America. The concrete commitment is to organise the programme and international engagement for 18–20 October 2027. The economic case they make is that sizable investment and banking links already exist, while payments and settlement across the two regions still depend on how institutions connect. The release sets out opportunities for infrastructure and business development. It does not announce a fund, specify investment commitments or put a cross-border payment service into operation.

The scale of existing ties matters for judging the proposition. The release cites Spanish ministry data putting Spain’s stock of direct investment in Latin America at nearly US$229 billion in 2024. It cites 744 foreign companies using Spain as a regional investment platform, controlling 1,081 subsidiaries. Banco de España estimates that about one-quarter of Spanish banks’ total assets are in Latin America, particularly Mexico and Brazil. Those figures measure three different things: a stock of direct investment, a network of affiliated companies, and bank balance sheets. They indicate a potential constituency for better financial links. None measures how much additional capital the summit itself will mobilise.

Payments provide the authors’ clearest illustration of what could change. They point to plans by European providers including Bizum to connect domestic systems and to the ECB’s feasibility assessment of linking the Eurosystem’s TIPS infrastructure with Brazil’s Pix. If the latter became operational, the release suggests that euro area–Brazil payments could become cheaper and faster. The assessment is still a study. Its benefits would depend on operating rules, participation and handling transactions that cross currencies and jurisdictions. For banks reliant on traditional cross-border processing, the distinction between a viable link and an announced intention is commercially important.

Programme topics include tokenised assets, digital money, stablecoins and settlement alongside cybersecurity, financial crime and prudential oversight. The organisers explicitly recognise that better integration could create dependencies if critical technology is concentrated. They also plan to connect fintech companies with financial institutions and investors, consider the financing of digital infrastructure, and discuss access to services and skills. Approximately 2,000 participants are expected. Attendance and opportunities to demonstrate products will be easier to observe than durable capital commitments or lower costs to end users.

The partners contribute different assets. Banco de España offers institutional relationships and regulatory expertise. GFTN, which MAS established as a not-for-profit in 2024, brings industry contacts and experience organising forums. Governor José Luis Escrivá presents the goal as converting existing relationships into practical projects while safeguarding stability. GFTN’s leadership stresses connectivity across networks. Annual editions remain subject to further agreement. The strongest inference for investors is therefore about which cross-border frictions the institutions want to address and whom they can convene. The release supplies no basis for projecting transaction volumes, future fee income or returns to a particular operator.

questions.question: Which proposed payment connection would produce measurable savings for customers?
questions.detail: The release identifies TIPS–Pix feasibility work and European network plans, but supplies no corridor-level costs, volumes or target service levels. For payment providers’ revenue exposure, compare official feasibility work and eventual operating rules with banks’ existing charges, FX spreads and settlement times. Determine which intermediary costs disappear and which persist because of foreign exchange, compliance or liquidity requirements.

questions.question: Could an existing relationship translate into genuinely additional investment?
questions.detail: The direct-investment stock, number of subsidiaries and banking exposures describe an established network. They do not identify capital a new venture could attract. Review project announcements, investor mandates, financing terms and the identity of the party taking risk. An opportunity financed entirely by shifting existing funds would have a different effect on credit demand and earnings than a newly funded project.

questions.question: Who would bear the cost of interoperability and responsibility for disruptions?
questions.detail: Connecting systems can create shared dependencies even if both domestic networks work well. Examine published governance proposals, provider contracts, incident responsibilities and regulatory assessments for the specific link. Compare the investment required of a bank with its potential transaction volumes and margins to assess where gains from cheaper cross-border service could accrue.

limitation: The source is the signed partnership announcement. It describes plans for a summit, rather than executed infrastructure projects or committed investment.
